partial_case.facts: The resident's tenancy of the property, a one-bedroom house, began in August 2022. She was 19 years old and had been homeless and living in hostels since the age of 16. This was her first tenancy and the first time she would be living alone. In July 2024 she complained to the landlord that it had not completed various repairs, most of which she reported around the time her tenancy began. She said this included a fence which she had since replaced at her own expense. The resident complained to the landlord that when her tenancy began in August 2022, there were numerous outstanding repair issues that it took a long time to resolve or had not yet resolved. This included flooring in the hall and stairs, a missing bedroom door, guttering and a damaged fence. She explained the fence had become further damaged and the landlord told her it would take tenancy enforcement action against her if she did not repair it. She informed it that since submitting her complaint, she had spent £1,618 repairing the fence and asked it to reimburse her.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord did not complete numerous repairs within 28 days as required by its repairs policy. While it acknowledged this in its complaint responses, it has still not fully completed all the repairs.
As the landlord failed to repair the fence during void stage, it should have compensated the resident for the full costs she incurred when she later replaced it.

Given that almost a year has passed since the landlord issued its stage 2 response and a number of repair issues remain unresolved, we are unable to find that it provided reasonable redress to the complaint.

partial_case.facts: The resident’s assured tenancy of a one-bedroom house began in August 2022. The resident was 19 years old, had been homeless and living in hostels since age 16, and this was her first tenancy and first time living alone. In July 2024, the resident complained to the landlord that various repairs had not been completed, most of which she reported around the start of the tenancy; she also said this included a fence she had replaced at her own expense. The complaint concerned handling of repairs, the resident’s request for reimbursement of fencing costs, and complaint handling. The resident said outstanding or unresolved repair issues included flooring in the hall and stairs, a missing bedroom door, guttering, a damaged fence, drainage/toilet problems, bathroom ventilation, windows, heating, and pests in the attic. The resident told the landlord she had spent £1,618 repairing the fence and asked it to reimburse her. The landlord’s stage 1 response offered £1,850 compensation, including £1,350 for repair delays, £500 for failure to repair the fence, and £100 for the late complaint response. The landlord’s stage 2 response upheld its stage 1 findings and offered an additional £50 for delay in issuing the stage 2 response. The resident asked the Ombudsman to investigate, saying repairs remained outstanding and pest proofing had not been completed.

orders: Payment of £3,818 made up of £600 for repairs maladministration, £100 for reimbursement-request service failure, £1,118 reimbursement for fence replacement costs, and £2,000 compensation offered in complaint responses
Inspection and written survey report/action plan

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord did not complete numerous repairs within 28 days as required by its repairs policy. While it acknowledged this in its complaint responses, it has still not fully completed all the repairs.
As the landlord failed to repair the fence during void stage, it should have compensated the resident for the full costs she incurred when she later replaced it.

Given that almost a year has passed since the landlord issued its stage 2 response and a number of repair issues remain unresolved, we are unable to find that it provided reasonable redress to the complaint.
Instead, we find that there was maladministration in its handling of repairs.
This was not reasonable in our view and it should have offered to reimburse her the full cost of the fence.
That it did not was service failure.
Therefore, in our view, it is fair that it should fully compensate the resident for the fencing costs. As it has already paid £500, we have ordered it to pay her the £1,118 remaining balance.
We therefore find the landlord provided reasonable redress to its failure to respond to the complaint within appropriate timeframes.
